articles.title: Semana Farroupilha reúne tradição, dança e gastronomia em Palhoça | G1
articles.standfirst: Programação no Lago da Pedra Branca acontece até 20 de setembro.
articles.summary: Programação no Lago da Pedra Branca, em Palhoça, acontece até 20 de setembro.
articles.body:
Palhoça , na Grande Florianópolis, recebe entre este sábado (12) e 20 de setembro a Semana Farroupilha Pedra Branca , evento gratuito que promete reunir a tradição, a cultura e a gastronomia gaúcha ao longo de nove dias de programação.

O festival ocorre no Lago da Pedra Branca e contará com mais de 40 atrações, incluindo shows, bailes, apresentações folclóricas, feira de artesanato e atividades destinadas a públicos de todas as idades (confira mais abaixo a programação do primeiro final de semana da celebração ).

A abertura da festividade traz ritos tradicionais do movimento gaucho, como a chegada da Chama Crioula e cerimônias oficiais com a participação de Centros de Tradições Gaúchas (CTGs) de toda a região.

O público poderá assistir a apresentações de invernadas artísticas de dança, declamações de poesia e shows de música nativista. Entre os nomes confirmados no palco principal estão os artistas Carlos Magrão, Galopaço, Grupo Fronteiras, Arrasta Coração, Ivan Mascarenhas e a banda Legião Gaúcha.

Na área gastronômica, o grande destaque da estrutura é o churrasco assado à moda antiga, com cortes de costela na ripa, entrecôte e contrafilé preparados na hora.

O evento também contará com encontros gastronômicos beneficentes, como o 10° Costelaço do Gringo no domingo (13), o Entrevero Solidário (no dia 19) e o Costelaço Solidário, que encerra a programação no dia 20.

A programação de segunda a sexta-feira oferecerá aulas gratuitas de danças gaúchas ministradas pelo professor Jackson Mattia e pelo grupo Família Arte Nativa. As oficinas abordarão ritmos como vanera, xote, bugio, milonga, chamamé, valsa, marcha e rancheira. A atividade é aberta para todas as idades, e as inscrições antecipadas podem ser realizadas pelo endereço oficial do evento .

Diariamente, ao final da tarde, o Galpão Nativo sediará o projeto "Entardecer na Querência", um espaço de convivência inspirado no encerramento das lidas campeiras. O local abrigará rodas de chimarrão e apresentações acústicas com voz, violão e gaita. Para garantir a experiência aos frequentadores, haverá distribuição gratuita de água quente e erva-mate no espaço.

A realização da Semana Farroupilha reúne a Associação Amigos e Organizadores de Cavalgada, Movimento Tradicionalista Gaúcho de Santa Catarina (MTG-SC), entidades como o Lions Club e Rotary Club de Palhoça Pedra Branca, além de diversos CTGs da Grande Florianópolis.

Programação da Semana Farroupilha Pedra Branca

16h: Apresentações culturais com Nelton Claro e Grupo

17h: Encontro e Mostra Tradicionalista com Ilha Xucra, Querência Açoriana e Grupo dos Oito (danças, canto, chula e pajadas)

18h: Abertura oficial da Semana Farroupilha com Chegada da Chama Crioula e Entrada das Bandeiras (participação de CTGs locais, MTG-SC e Amigos de Cavalgadas)

19h: Apresentação especial da Invernada Artística do CTG Os Praianos (Dança da Jardineira e Dança do Pau de Fita)

20h: Baile com Adriano Ataide Mestre Juvenil e Banda

9h: Abertura com feira de artesanato, parque infantil e Chimarreando com Amigos no Galpão Nativo com Nelton Caro (água quente e erva-mate gratuitas)

11h30 às 15h: 10º Costelaço do Gringo e Amigos Pedra Branca e Churrasco à Moda Antiga comandado pelo “Polenta”

12h: Gaiteraço (encontro de gaiteiros no Palco Farroupilha)

13h: Show com Fabrício Luiz e Fabrício Júnior

17h: Apresentação da Invernada Artística do CTG Os Praianos

articles.title: Casal de idosos fica ferido após muro ceder e atingir casa enquanto dormia no interior de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu em Jacupiranga durante a madrugada deste sábado (12), quando fortes rajadas de vento atingiram o Vale do Ribeira. Imóvel precisou ser interditado.
articles.summary: Acidente aconteceu em Jacupiranga durante a madrugada deste sábado (12), quando fortes rajadas de vento atingiram o Vale do Ribeira. Imóvel precisou ser interditado.
articles.body:
Casal de idosos fica ferido após muro ceder e atingir casa enquanto dormia — Foto: TV Tribuna

Um casal de idosos ficou ferido após um muro ceder e atingir o imóvel enquanto eles dormiam, em Jacupiranga (SP), na madrugada deste sábado (12). O acidente aconteceu durante as fortes rajadas de vento que atingiram o Vale do Ribeira.

A residência fica no bairro Botujuru, em um nível mais baixo em relação a um barranco. Conforme apurado pela reportagem, o muro ficava acima da área onde está o quarto das vítimas e cedeu por volta das 2h30. O local precisou ser interditado por segurança.

Com a queda, parte do muro e da terra atingiu a estrutura da casa. As circunstâncias que provocaram o desabamento ainda não foram informadas.

As duas vítimas foram levadas ao Pronto-Socorro de Jacupiranga. Uma delas já havia sido socorrida quando as equipes chegaram ao endereço, enquanto a outra apresentava ferimentos na perna. Os ferimentos foram considerados leves.

Não há registro de chuva em Jacupiranga relacionado à ocorrência. A cidade, no entanto, também foi atingida pelos fortes ventos registrados na região durante a madrugada.

De acordo com a Defesa Civil, a previsão é de tempo nublado a parcialmente nublado, com pancadas de chuva em praticamente todo o estado. As precipitações podem vir acompanhadas de raios, rajadas de vento e, de forma isolada, granizo.

O órgão informou que acompanha a evolução das condições meteorológicas por meio de radares, satélites, descargas atmosféricas e observações de superfície. As faixas leste e sul do estado, incluindo a Baixada Santista, devem concentrar os maiores volumes de chuva.

Durante tempestades, a Defesa Civil recomenda:

evitar áreas abertas, árvores, postes e estruturas metálicas;

afastar-se de coberturas, placas e estruturas vulneráveis durante rajadas fortes;

em caso de granizo, permanecer em local coberto e protegido, afastado de janelas;

não atravessar áreas alagadas ou com correnteza;

acompanhar os alertas oficiais da Defesa Civil.

articles.title: Elefante Sandro entra em caixa para transporte ao Santuário de MT | G1
articles.standfirst: Operação começou nesta quinta-feira (10) e equipe do Santuário vai posicionar a caixa de transporte dentro do recinto onde fica o elefante, no Zoológico Municipal Quinzinho de Barros.
articles.summary: O elefante Sandro iniciou a adaptação na caixa de transporte para ser levado do Zoológico de Sorocaba ao Santuário de Elefantes Brasil, no Mato Grosso.
articles.body:
O elefante Sandro deu o primeiro passo para sua transferência do Zoológico Municipal Quinzinho de Barros, em Sorocaba (SP), para o Santuário de Elefantes Brasil (SEB), na Chapada dos Guimarães (MT). O animal entrou neste sábado (12) voluntariamente na caixa especial instalada em seu recinto para reconhecer a nova estrutura.

A caixa de transporte chegou ao parque na tarde de quinta-feira (10) e foi posicionada na área externa na noite de sexta-feira (11), após trabalho de nivelamento do solo que durou mais de seis horas.

Sandro, que tem idade estimada em 54 anos, e desde 1982 vive no zoo de Sorocaba , entrou na estrutura nesta manhã. Veja no vídeo acima .

Elefante Sandro entra em caixa de transporte no zoo de Sorocaba (SP) e inicia adaptação para viagem ao Santuário de MT — Foto: Andre Rosa/SEB

Segundo o presidente do Santuário dos Elefantes do Brasil (SEB), Raphael Bontempi Ferreira, a aproximação inicial ocorreu por curiosidade natural do animal diante do novo objeto. O veterinário responsável pelo zoológico, André Costa, explicou que o processo é acompanhado de perto para garantir o menor nível possível de estresse.

"Ele está acostumado com pessoas. Claro que quando faz qualquer tipo de interferência no recinto, ele já sente muita estranheza. Mas a gente imagina que ele se adapte bem", afirmou.

A caixa metálica possui janelas de ventilação, sensores térmicos e dimensões adaptadas para o porte do animal.

A caixa que será usada para o transporte do elefante Sandro tem aproximadamente dez toneladas, cinco metros de comprimento, 3,5 metros de altura e 2,5 de largura. A estrutura também conta com sistema de monitoramento de temperatura e janelas para ventilação.

O trajeto de Sandro para o centro-oeste brasileiro é de aproximadamente 1.615 km de estrada, em uma viagem de dois dias e meio.

Caixa tem aproximadamente dez toneladas, cinco metros de comprimento, 3,5 metros de altura e 2,5 de largura — Foto: Thiago Ariosi / TV TEM

A adaptação de Sandro à caixa pode levar de cinco a sete dias, mas esse prazo pode ser ampliado. Tudo vai depender de como ele vai responder. Somente quando ele estiver pronto é que vai começar a transferência.

Elefante Sandro tem 54 anos e vive no zoo de Sorocaba (SP) há 44 anos — Foto: Luan Lima/Arquivo Pessoal

A equipe de veterinários que comandará a viagem do elefante deve usar técnicas de reforço positivo para que ele se familiarize com a estrutura. O processo de adaptação deve ocorrer da seguinte forma:

A caixa será colocada na área que o elefante habita, ficando aberta para que ele acesse o espaço e se acostume com o ambiente por alguns dias;

A equipe veterinária irá acompanhar o comportamento de Sandro, analisando a aproximação dele com a caixa e o comportamento ao ficar dentro dela, com as portas fechadas, em alguns momentos durante o dia;

A partir da adaptação do elefante ao objeto, a transferência será iniciada com apoio de um caminhão para o transporte da carga viva.

Equipe vai posicionar caixa de transporte dentro do recinto do elefante Sandro — Foto: TV TEM / Reprodução

O Santuário dos Elefantes deve cumprir a transferência de Sandro até o final de setembro.

Contrária à medida judicial, a Prefeitura de Sorocaba informou que que "prestará todo o apoio institucional e técnico à operação de transferência do elefante ao Santuário, dentro das atribuições que competem ao Parque Zoológico Municipal Quinzinho de Barros".

O candidato ao Governo da Paraíba pelo Democracia Cristã (DC), Pedro Coutinho, afirmou que pretende ter uma política de diálogo com municípios para impulsionar o turismo no estado. A declaração foi dada em entrevista à TV Cabo Branco.

articles.title: 'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves
articles.summary: Consumer group Which? has called the sale of jack mackerel, a cheaper, less nutritious species of fish, an example of "skimpflation".
articles.body:
A growing trend of supermarkets selling a cheaper, less nutritious alternative to tinned mackerel is an example of "skimpflation", a consumer group has said.

Princes - which supplies major supermarkets - has substituted jack mackerel, an entirely different species, for mackerel, with similar tins also being sold by Lidl.

The switch has been spurred by dwindling stocks of Atlantic mackerel after years of overfishing, with its Chilean counterpart more sustainable and a third of the cost.

"It's a real concern when manufacturers quietly downgrade everyday staples like these as shoppers can end up paying the same price for a product that delivers significantly less nutritional quality," Sue Davies, head of food policy at Which?, said.

Jack mackerel contains about half as much omega-3 and around a third as much vitamin B12 as traditional mackerel.

The shift has prompted complaints from some consumers over differences in taste and texture, as well as concerns about how clearly the replacement fish is being labelled.

Princes announced last October that it was changing all of its tinned mackerel products to jack mackerel, saying the species meets the Marine Stewardship Council's sustainability standards.

The firm said its jack mackerel products were "clearly identified" and had been introduced following extensive product and consumer testing, describing it as having a "milder flavour and meatier texture".

Lidl is selling jack mackerel under its house brand. Lidl GB said it was "committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries".

Davies from Which? said: "While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product's recipe."

She added: "Skimpflation - quietly changing ingredients to cut costs - has become increasingly common, but it can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it."

Despite its name, jack mackerel is not a type of mackerel. Jack mackerel belongs to the Carangidae fish family, while traditional mackerel belongs to the Scombridae family.

Until December 2025, under UK law, Carangidae species could only be marketed as "jack", "scad", "trevally" or "horse mackerel".

But shortly after Princes launched its new product as "jack mackerel", the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs changed its rules to permit the labelling.

Industry figures reposted by seafood market intelligence platform Undercurrent suggest wholesale Chilean jack mackerel costs roughly one-third as much as Atlantic mackerel.

The Scottish Pelagic Fishermen's Association said there was the potential for confusion, saying "consumers should be able to clearly understand what they are buying".

CEO designate Hannah Fennell said: "If retailers move away from Northeast Atlantic mackerel, they are unfairly punishing the UK industry while instead sourcing a different, less omega-3-rich species from the other side of the world with a significantly higher carbon footprint to the UK market."

The switch follows the so-called "mackerel war", a long-running dispute between the UK, Iceland, Greenland, Norway, the Faroe Islands, the EU and Russia over shared mackerel catch quotas.

The countries have repeatedly failed to agree a unified system for sharing stock and setting catch limits in line with scientific advice.

Mackerel catches in the north-east Atlantic have exceeded the levels advised by scientists by an average of 39% over the past 15 years, according to the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC).

Stocks have plummeted by roughly three-quarters over the past decade, according to the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (Ices).

The intergovernmental body has advised slashing the quantity of north-east Atlantic mackerel caught in 2026 by roughly 70% to allow the stock a chance to recover.

Last year, the Marine Conservation Society said the Atlantic mackerel population was at "breaking point".

The severe depletion of mackerel numbers has led to the fish losing its MSC certification, meaning it no longer complies with many retailers' sustainability policies. Chilean jack mackerel, in contrast, is MSC-certified.

In February, Waitrose said it would suspend sales of fresh, chilled and frozen mackerel due to overfishing concerns, while tinned products would be phased out as existing stock was sold.

The Marine Conservation Society heralded the move as "leading and decisive".

The switch to jack mackerel is being felt beyond the UK, with supermarkets in the Netherlands no longer selling Atlantic mackerel and at least one supermarket in Sweden switching to jack mackerel.

articles.title: Nationwide protests in Germany draw tens of thousands after AfD win
articles.summary: Tens of thousands demonstrated across Germany against far-right extremism on Saturday, with major rallies held in Dusseldorf, Hamburg, Berlin and Munich, alm...
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people across Germany protested against far-right extremism following the AfD party's historic election win in Saxony-Anhalt.

Major rallies were held in Dusseldorf, Hamburg, Berlin, and Munich, with participants demanding a review of parties suspected of being far-right extremist by Germany's domestic intelligence agency.

The AfD, monitored nationwide as a suspected extremist organization, saw its state branches in Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt classified as far-right extremist, prompting discussions about a potential ban on the party.

Tens of thousands demonstrated across Germany against far-right extremism on Saturday, with major rallies held in Dusseldorf, Hamburg, Berlin and Munich, almost a week after the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's historic election win.

Sunday's election win for the AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election, where they earned 44% of the vote, brought Germany's far right closest yet to gaining power since World War II.

In Dusseldorf, around 20,000 people took part in a protest march "against the AfD and right-wing hatred," according to police and organizers, while organizers said a further 25,000 marched in Hamburg.

In Berlin, several marches against the normalization of right-wing politics converged on the city's town hall. Police put the number of participants at 18,000, while organizers said 32,000 took part.

In several cities, rallies were also held as part of the nationwide initiative demanding that Germany's Constitutional Court review parties suspected of being or confirmed to be far-right extremist by Germany's domestic intelligence agency. These demonstrations, organized by the group PRÜF, which translates as proof or check, take place on the second Saturday of each month in German state capitals.

The largest of these rallies on Saturday was in Munich, where police said around 12,000 people gathered. Around 2,000 came together in Mainz, around 1,500 in Saarbrücken and around 1,100 in Magdeburg. Protests were also held in Leipzig and Saarbrücken.

The AfD is monitored nationwide by the domestic intelligence agency as a suspected extremist organization. Several of its state branches, including those in Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, are classified as far-right extremist.

Following the AfD's election success in Saxony-Anhalt, North Rhine-Westphalia state premier Hendrik Wüst proposed setting up a joint federal-state working group to examine whether a ban on the party could be pursued. The proposal has won support from some politicians but has also met with scepticism.

Only the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, the Bundesrat, the upper house, or the federal government can apply to the Federal Constitutional Court for a party to be banned. Any ban would be decided by this court.

articles.title: Georgia police officer who killed 1-year-old donkey HeeHaw says the miniature donkey charged at him; owner says 'he was my kid'
articles.summary: US News: A Georgia police officer who shot and killed a beloved pet donkey while searching for a missing 12-year-old girl has explained why he opened fire, say.
articles.body: A Georgia police officer who shot and killed a beloved pet donkey while searching for a missing 12-year-old girl has explained why he opened fire, saying the animal charged at officers and did not stop even after a Taser was used.The donkey, named HeeHaw, was a one-year-old bottle-raised animal kept as a family pet at Elsberry Riding and Farm in Rockmart, Georgia. His death on August 30 triggered widespread outrage after the owner said he was friendly, harmless and had never shown aggression toward people.A newly released police report provides the first detailed account from Cedartown Police Officer Trenton Garner, who was involved in the search for the missing girl.What happened to HeeHaw?According to Garner's report, officers were searching for the 12-year-old girl shortly after midnight on August 30. A K-9 handler and a bloodhound team were following a trail of footprints when they entered the property.Garner said the team followed the trail toward a petting zoo and pasture area. As they moved along a fence line, horses in the pasture became startled and ran away.The officers then spotted HeeHaw.Garner said the donkey began moving toward the officers and then charged at them.The K-9 handler reportedly pulled out a Taser and aimed it at the animal. According to Garner, the Taser failed to stop HeeHaw.Garner then drew his department-issued Glock 17 and fired a single shot.The donkey was struck and ran up a hill before collapsing, according to the police report.Officer says he feared the donkeyGarner's account is that he fired because he believed HeeHaw posed a threat to the officers.The police report says the team was moving through the property while trying to locate the missing girl and that the donkey's behavior prompted the officers to respond with force.The incident was also captured by a drone being operated by Rockmart firefighters, according to reports.The missing girl was eventually found safe at a church near the area where officers were searching.Owner disputes police accountHeeHaw's owner, Hannah Israel, has strongly disputed the suggestion that the donkey was dangerous. Israel said HeeHaw had been bottle-raised and was accustomed to people because he had been used in petting zoos. She described him as a beloved family animal who had never shown aggression toward strangers.She has also questioned why officers entered the property and pasture without notifying the family or obtaining permission. Israel said HeeHaw was simply reacting to strangers entering his territory when he approached and brayed. The family has been left devastated by the shooting and has sought accountability over the incident.What happened to the police officer?Garner has been placed on administrative leave while the shooting is investigated.The Cedartown Police Department confirmed that an investigation was underway. The Georgia Department of Agriculture Law Enforcement Division is also conducting an independent investigation into the shooting. The incident has generated significant public reaction, with many people questioning whether deadly force was justified against the donkey and demanding the release of body-camera footage.Israel has also shared videos of HeeHaw from before his death, showing the animal at the farm.She has urged people not to threaten the officer or others involved, while continuing to seek accountability through legal channels.Why was HeeHaw on the property?The donkey was not connected to the missing-child case.Police were searching the area after the 12-year-old girl went missing. Officers followed a trail during the search that led them onto the farm property. The girl was later found safe near a church. HeeHaw was encountered during that search and was shot after the officer said the animal charged at the team.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Indian academic in UK for 60 yrs missing in Nepal floods; Brit MP says country refused help
articles.summary: South Asia News: An Indian academic who has lived in Britain for more than 60 years has become the subject of a pointed debate in the UK parliament after disappearing .
articles.body: An Indian academic who has lived in Britain for more than 60 years has become the subject of a pointed debate in the UK parliament after disappearing in Nepal’s Aug 26 floods, with his constituency's MP in that country alleging that authorities declined to assist in his case because he did not hold a British passport.Dr Anirban Bhattacharyya, 66, of Newbiggin-by-the-Sea in northeast England, remains on Nepal Police’s official missing-persons list more than two weeks after the disaster. A research associate at Newcastle University’s School of Computing, he held degrees from King’s College London and South Bank Polytechnic, and had completed his PhD at Newcastle University in 2013.Raising the case during Business Questions in the House of Commons, Ashington and Blyth MP Ian Lavery said, “Dr Anirban Bhattacharyya is a resident in my constituency. He has lived there for 60 years. He travelled to Kolkata only a couple of weeks ago, and it appears that he has been caught up in the horrendous flooding in Nepal.”Lavery said repeated attempts to contact Bhattacharyya had failed. “There have been numerous attempts to contact him, but they have been unsuccessful. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (London) has been less than helpful, basically pointing the family to the Indian consulate...,” he told Parliament.The British MP also questioned why Bhattacharyya’s six decades in Britain counted for little because he had retained Indian citizenship. “He has lived in this country for 60 years. He is missing. Can we have a debate about how the FCDO can be more helpful to people who have lived in this country all their lives and are affected by such national tragedies? Because he does not have a British passport, we cannot help him.”In a subsequent social-media post, Lavery said FCDO had told the family it could not assist because Bhattacharyya held an Indian passport and had instead referred them to Indian authorities. He said he wanted a wider debate on how Britain supports long-term residents without citizenship and hoped to secure a ministerial meeting to seek answers for the family.Responding in the Commons, leader of House Alan Campbell said, “We are working with authorities on the ground to support their efforts in this terrible situation, supporting survivors of all nationalities and trying to get information for families about missing loved ones.”He added, “We are also in contact with the Indian authorities about the relief effort. I am disappointed that that has not led to the outcome that my honourable friend seeks. I will see if the relevant minister will meet with him to discuss this case and wider issues about what govts can do in what are often terrible circumstances.”Bhattacharyya was travelling with Kolkata-based Chalo Jaai Travel Club on a Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage handled in Nepal by Samrat Tours and Travels and remains among 32 members of the contingent — 30 tourists and two tour employees — who are still missing near Timure-Rasuwagadhi. Nepal immigration records showed members of the group had cleared immigration shortly before the flood struck, leaving uncertainty over whether they had crossed into Tibet or remained near the border when the torrent arrived.Bhattacharyya’s family friend has turned to Nepal’s mountaineering community for help, posting an appeal with his photograph and details of his last known movements on a forum followed by trekkers, tour operators and mountain guides.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Ten people were evacuated from the home in Araucanía region in central Chile.
articles.body:
At least 16 elderly residents have died in a fire at a nursing home in Chile, according to authorities.

Ten others were evacuated after a blaze broke out at El Edén home in /idt2/d9cfcc9a-2842-463f-a4d8-4dd007ef9547, around 640km (400 miles) south of the capital Santiago, on Friday evening.

Jorge Granada, a prosecutor leading the case, said it was not clear at this stage what caused the incident.

Chile's President José Antonio Kast said he had ordered a review into the condition of nursing homes across the country.

"We will fully collaborate with the justice system to clarify what happened, determine where failures may have existed in oversight or prevention, identify what alerts were raised and what actions were taken in response to them," Kast said.

articles.title: In 1926, beekeeper Ruth Suckow published Iowa Interiors, a small-town story collection that made her nationally known; 100 years later, a Cedar Falls press is reviving the hard-to-find book
articles.summary: US News: In 1926, Iowa writer Ruth Suckow published Iowa Interiors, a collection of 14 short stories drawn from the lives of people in the state’s farms and sm.
articles.body: In 1926, Iowa writer Ruth Suckow published Iowa Interiors, a collection of 14 short stories drawn from the lives of people in the state’s farms and small towns. A century later, the book is returning to print in a new centennial edition from Cedar Falls-based Final Thursday Press, with new illustrations by Iowa artist Claudia McGehee. The Hearst Center for the Arts in Cedar Falls is marking the anniversary with an exhibition of McGehee’s original illustrations, running September 10 through December 6. The exhibition is part of a broader effort to bring Suckow’s work back to readers. Suckow was already an established writer when Iowa Interiors appeared. Her first novel, Country People, had been published in 1924, followed by The Odyssey of a Nice Girl in 1925. Iowa Interiors, published by Alfred A. Knopf, further established her reputation and has since become one of the works most closely associated with her portrayals of Iowa life.The beekeeper who became a chronicler of IowaBefore her literary career fully took hold, Suckow had an unusual occupation for a writer: beekeeping. She spent years in Earlville, Iowa, where she managed the Orchard Apiary. A 1930 Time profile described her as the manager-owner of the apiary, which she operated for six years. Suckow’s connection with Earlville would become an important part of her life and literary history.Her fiction focused on the people she observed around her, farmers, families, renters, ministers and residents of small communities. Iowa Interiors contains stories such as “A Start in Life,” “A Homecoming,” “Uprooted,” “Renters” and “A Rural Community,” depicting the pressures and changes shaping everyday life in early 20th-century Iowa. The complete original collection runs 283 pages. The Hearst Center describes the 1926 collection as the work that established Suckow’s national reputation.A century-old book gets another lifeFor today’s readers, one obstacle has been finding Suckow’s books in the first place. The Ruth Suckow Memorial Association says copies of Iowa Interiors have become increasingly difficult to find. The association has made many of the original stories available online while preparing for the new edition.The centennial edition is intended to change that. Final Thursday Press is publishing the new volume, edited by Julie Husband and Jim O’Loughlin. It will include a new introduction as well as illustrations commissioned from Claudia McGehee, whose work is being displayed at the Hearst Center alongside the anniversary celebration.McGehee has created 14 scratchboard illustrations, one for each story in the collection. The exhibition gives visitors a chance to see the original artwork while revisiting the world Suckow captured a century ago.Why Iowa Interiors still mattersSuckow’s Iowa was markedly different from the state of 2026. Her stories emerged from a world of small farms, village communities and economic constraints, rather than the large-scale agricultural landscape that dominates much of Iowa today. But the subjects of her fiction are less distant: people trying to make a living, maintain families, find independence and adjust to communities changing around them.That is part of what the editors of the new edition hope readers will rediscover. Rather than treating Iowa Interiors simply as a historical record, the centennial project presents it as literature that can still speak to contemporary readers. A century after its first publication, the book is therefore returning to the place and literary tradition that shaped it, giving a new generation a chance to meet the Iowa that Suckow saw, one ordinary life at a time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Proposal of $100K OPT fee clears White House review: Here's what happens next?
articles.summary: US News: International students in the US are staring at a dramatic increase in the cost of working after graduation under a Trump administration proposal that.
articles.body: International students in the US are staring at a dramatic increase in the cost of working after graduation under a Trump administration proposal that has cleared the White House review. The proposal will soon become a rule and a $100,000 fee will be imposed for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program.OPT is a temporary work programme that allows eligible F-1 international students to gain practical work experience related to their field of study in the US.Students generally receive permission to work for up to 12 months after completing their academic programme. Those who graduate in qualifying science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields can receive a 24-month extension, allowing them to work for up to three years in total.OPT is particularly important for international students because it provides a bridge between graduation and employment-based immigration, including the H-1B programme.Around 300,000 F-1 students had employment authorization through OPT last year, according to Bloomberg Law.Would students have to pay $100,000?That remains unclear. The DHS proposal does not publicly disclose the amount or explain who would ultimately be responsible for paying the proposed fee. Many legal experts believe that the universities may have to pay it to the employers who hires its students for the OPT program. OPT $100,000 fee has cleared White House review and will be posted as a rule any day now. "Universities will be the ones to pay it, which makes no sense because why would they pay a fee for some random employer?" policy commentator Sam Peak said.Why would this matter to Indian students?If a student is expected to pay the fee, a $100,000 OPT fee could have a major impact on international students, particularly those who rely on OPT as their first opportunity to work in the US after completing a degree. For many Indian students, OPT is also an important route toward an H-1B petition. Students can use the OPT period to gain US work experience while an employer seeks to sponsor them for an H-1B visa. A six-figure fee could therefore affect not only students but also universities and employers that depend on international graduates.Indian American Advocacy Council co-founder Sidharth said if universities will have to pay this fee, they will admit fewer international students."International students will take their tuition, talent and research elsewhere. Graduate STEM programs will get hit. American employers will lose one of their biggest pipelines of US-educated talent and universities already facing enrollment pressure will lose billions more," he said."This isn't just an immigration restriction. It risks turning an international student from an asset universities compete to recruit into a six-figure financial liability after graduation, that changes the economics of American higher education overnight. articles.title: Meet Kelly Liu: The 16-year-old San Jose student who used AI to map dirty air, put pollution sensors in underserved schools and helped push a countywide policy change
articles.summary: US News: When Kelly Liu looked at air pollution data around San Jose, she noticed something important was missing. Official monitoring stations could show broa.
articles.body: When Kelly Liu looked at air pollution data around San Jose, she noticed something important was missing. Official monitoring stations could show broad regional trends, but they did not always reveal what students were breathing beside busy roads, industrial areas or older school buildings. The 16-year-old student decided to fill that gap by combining artificial intelligence, low-cost pollution sensors and community organising. Her work mapped local air quality, brought monitoring devices to underserved schools and helped build pressure for stronger countywide action. As described by Action for Nature and reported by Hoodline, Kelly’s project grew from a technical experiment into a public campaign, showing how student-led research can make environmental inequality visible and influence policy. Her story is not just about measuring dirty air. It is about giving communities evidence they can use to demand healthier places to learn.Seeing what broad data missesAir pollution rarely affects every neighbourhood in the same way. Two schools only a few miles apart may face very different conditions depending on their proximity to highways, warehouses, factories, construction sites or heavily travelled roads. Weather, traffic patterns and building ventilation can also influence the air students breathe during the school day.Traditional monitoring networks are valuable, but their stations are expensive and widely spaced. One monitor may represent conditions across a large area without capturing pollution hotspots near a particular campus. For families and teachers, that can create a frustrating gap between official regional data and their everyday experience.Kelly became interested in that gap while studying air quality in the South Bay. She wanted to understand where pollution was concentrated and whether some schools were receiving less protection than others. Rather than treating available data as complete, she asked what it left out.Using AI to map pollutionKelly used artificial intelligence as a tool for analysing and visualising complex environmental information. By combining available air quality records with location data, traffic patterns and other geographic indicators, she developed maps that could show likely pollution burdens at a more local level.The purpose of AI was not to replace scientific monitoring. It was to help identify patterns, compare communities and direct attention toward places that might deserve closer investigation. Algorithms can process large amounts of information much faster than a person working manually, making it easier to examine relationships between pollution, roadways, school locations and neighbourhood characteristics.The resulting maps helped turn an abstract issue into something people could see. Instead of discussing air quality only through countywide averages, Kelly could show how exposure might vary from one school to another. That visual clarity made the issue more accessible to students, parents, school administrators and policymakers.Still, maps based on models and existing records have limitations. They can suggest where pollution may be high, but sensors are needed to confirm conditions on the ground. Kelly’s work therefore moved beyond digital analysis and into direct community monitoring.Bringing sensors to underserved schoolsKelly helped place pollution sensors at schools in communities that are often underrepresented in environmental data. These devices can measure factors such as particulate matter, which includes tiny airborne particles capable of entering the lungs. Depending on the equipment, sensors may also track other pollutants or environmental conditions that affect indoor and outdoor air quality.Installing monitors at schools provides a more detailed picture of what students encounter. It can reveal changes during morning drop off, afternoon traffic, nearby construction or wildfire smoke events. It can also help schools understand whether filtration, ventilation and building maintenance are reducing exposure indoors.The focus on underserved schools was central to Kelly’s approach. Environmental monitoring is not only a technical challenge. It is also a question of fairness. Communities with fewer resources may face greater exposure to pollution while having less access to data, medical guidance or political influence. Placing sensors in those schools helped address both problems by producing evidence and involving the people most affected.Students could see readings from their own campuses and connect the information to lessons in science, technology and health. That made air quality a local and tangible subject rather than a distant environmental issue.From evidence to advocacyCollecting data was only one part of Kelly’s work. She also helped communicate the findings and encourage action. Students, parents and community supporters used the information to argue that schools should have stronger air quality protections, including better filtration, monitoring and policies for days when outdoor pollution becomes dangerous.Student advocacy can be especially powerful because it connects policy decisions to the people who spend much of their day inside school buildings. Kelly and other young organisers were not presenting pollution as an abstract statistic. They were asking why some children should learn in environments with higher exposure and fewer safeguards.Their efforts helped push the conversation beyond individual school campuses toward countywide policy. A countywide approach can create consistent standards, reduce disparities between districts and make it easier to secure funding for monitoring and clean air equipment. It also recognises that pollution does not stop at school boundaries.Why school air mattersChildren are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because their lungs and bodies are still developing. They also breathe more air relative to their body size than adults and may spend many hours each day at school. Exposure to fine particles and other pollutants can aggravate asthma, contribute to respiratory problems and affect attendance and concentration.Schools have a practical role in reducing risk. High quality filtration, properly maintained ventilation systems, closed windows during severe pollution events and clear response plans can all help protect students. Outdoor activity policies may also need to account for air quality, especially during wildfire smoke or periods of heavy traffic pollution.Without monitoring, schools may not know when conditions are changing or whether their mitigation efforts are working. Kelly’s project brought attention to that need and showed how comparatively affordable sensors can complement official monitoring networks.A model for youth-led environmental scienceKelly’s work combines research, technology and public engagement in a way that is increasingly important for environmental problem solving. Young people are often portrayed as passive recipients of climate and pollution policy, but Kelly’s project shows them acting as investigators and advocates.Her approach also demonstrates that environmental science does not end with data collection. A map becomes more useful when people can understand it. A sensor becomes more valuable when its results guide a decision. A policy becomes stronger when it responds to evidence gathered from the communities it affects.Action for Nature’s Eco-Hero recognition highlights this combination of initiative and impact. Kelly did not simply build a technical project for a competition. She used technology to investigate an inequality, worked with communities facing exposure and helped move the discussion toward institutional change.The challenges aheadCountywide policy changes can provide a foundation, but implementation requires funding, staff and accountability. Sensors must be calibrated and maintained. Data must be interpreted carefully, particularly when low-cost devices are used. Schools need resources to upgrade filters, repair ventilation systems and respond to changing conditions.There is also a need to communicate results without creating unnecessary alarm. Pollution readings can fluctuate, and one measurement does not always establish a long term health risk. Schools and families need clear guidance explaining what the data mean and what actions are appropriate.Kelly’s work points toward a more transparent system in which schools regularly measure air quality, publish understandable information and prioritise improvements where exposure and vulnerability are greatest. That process would make environmental protection more responsive and equitable.A cleaner future begins with visibilityKelly Liu’s story begins with a simple observation: people cannot solve a problem they cannot see. By using AI to map pollution, sensors to gather local evidence and advocacy to bring the findings into policy discussions, she helped make school air quality visible.Her work also offers a practical lesson for other communities. Environmental change does not always start with a major institution or an expensive research programme. It can begin with a student asking better questions, gathering evidence and inviting others to act.For Kelly, the goal is not merely to produce impressive maps or install more monitors. It is to help ensure that every student, regardless of neighbourhood or school budget, has the chance to learn in clean and healthy air. That ambition has already taken her project from a San Jose classroom to a broader countywide conversation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bali bans Australian tourist Billy Aspinall for 10 years after CCTV allegedly captures public sex act; locals perform purifying rituals
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An Australian tourist has been deported from Bali and banned from entering Indonesia for 10 years after he was allegedly caught on CCTV engaging in a .
articles.body: An Australian tourist has been deported from Bali and banned from entering Indonesia for 10 years after he was allegedly caught on CCTV engaging in a sex act with a woman outside a residential property in North Kuta.Billy Aspinall, 27, from Queensland's Sunshine Coast, was arrested at Bali's I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport on August 25, three days after the alleged incident was recorded by a security camera in the Tibubeneng area of North Kuta.Aspinall had been trying to board a flight home to Brisbane when immigration officials stopped him. He subsequently spent about two weeks in immigration detention before being deported.Australian tourist deported to BrisbaneThe latest development was confirmed by Muhamad Novyandri, head of the Ngurah Rai Immigration Office, who said Aspinall was deported on Tuesday night on a Batik Air flight from Denpasar to Brisbane.“The deportation of BA was carried out on Tuesday night using a Batik Air flight on the Denpasar-Brisbane route,” Novyandri said, according to reports.The 10-year ban means Aspinall will not be allowed to enter Indonesia in any capacity during the period of the sanction.What happened on the Bali driveway?The incident took place on August 22 outside a residential property in Tibubeneng, North Kuta.CCTV footage allegedly showed Aspinall and a woman engaging in sexual activity on a driveway near the property's entrance. The woman has not been publicly identified and is believed to be another foreign tourist.According to reports, the woman had been drinking with Aspinall before the incident.A local woman reportedly came across the pair while she was on her way to pray. She was said to have shouted at them to stop, but they allegedly continued.The entire encounter reportedly lasted around 15 minutes before the pair left the property.The CCTV footage subsequently spread widely online, prompting anger among local residents.Police said incident could affect Bali's imageNorth Kuta chief police commander Ketut Sukadana said the alleged conduct had the potential to cause concern among residents.“The alleged indecent acts have the potential to cause public concern,” Sukadana said.He added that the incident could particularly affect residents of Tibubeneng and could harm the perception of safety and tourism in the North Kuta area if it were not addressed.Authorities said the matter needed to be handled seriously, including under local customary law or national law.Locals hold cleansing ceremonyThe incident also prompted a traditional response from residents.A cleansing ceremony was held at the property where the alleged incident took place, with locals seeking to purify the area and remove what they regarded as negative or bad energy following the incident.The reaction reflects the importance of local customs and community standards in Bali, a predominantly Hindu island that attracts millions of international tourists.What does Indonesian law say?The case comes after Indonesia brought its revised Criminal Code into force on January 2, 2026, introducing several changes to the country's criminal laws.The new provisions include offences relating to sex outside marriage and cohabitation, although legal experts have pointed out that such offences generally require a complaint from specific family members before authorities can prosecute.Legal expert Retno Murni, founder of the People's Law Center, said complaints involving alleged adultery or sex outside marriage can be filed only by certain relatives, including a legal husband or wife, parents or children of the person involved.She said foreign tourists therefore cannot simply be arrested or prosecuted for staying with a partner without the required complaint.Public indecency, however, is treated separately, and authorities have indicated that conduct in public places can trigger enforcement action.Murni advised tourists to respect Indonesian laws and local customs and to behave appropriately while visiting the country.Woman in CCTV footage remains unidentifiedWhile Aspinall has now been deported, authorities have not publicly identified the woman who allegedly appeared with him in the CCTV footage.Earlier, immigration officials said they would continue working with police to locate the woman and determine whether any immigration action should also be taken against her.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission Saturday met with the representatives of both factions of Trinamool Congress, one headed by former West Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee and the other group headed by West Bengal leader of opposition Ritabrata Banerjee, amid their competing claims to being the real party entitled to the use of its "twin flower" poll symbol.The meeting with EC, amid the dispute over the party's authorised signatories and organisational elections, gains significance as it comes ahead of the Nandigram and Rejinagar assembly bypolls scheduled for Oct 6. articles.title: Modi and Xi seek to end tensions with solution to border dispute
articles.summary: India and China are seeking a mutually acceptable solution to their border dispute, the government in New Delhi said, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Chi...
articles.body:
India and China are seeking a mutually acceptable solution to their border dispute, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi emphasizing the importance of peace and stability in the border areas during a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit in New Delhi.

Tensions between India and China have been ongoing since border skirmishes in 2020, with the two countries having a long-standing dispute over territory in the Himalayan mountain range.

Both countries agreed last year to work towards a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable" resolution of the border conflict, emphasizing the need to abide by previous agreements and understandings on border issues.

India and China are seeking a mutually acceptable solution to their border dispute, the government in New Delhi said, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in the Indian capital on Saturday.

According to India's Foreign Ministry, Modi stressed to Xi that peace and stability in the border areas between the two countries remained an essential foundation for the further development of bilateral relations. It is Xi's first visit to the neighbouring country in seven years.

Ties between the two countries have been tense since border skirmishes in 2020. The two nuclear powers have long disputed a territory in the Himalayan mountain range, which Beijing regards as part of southern Tibet and New Delhi considers part of the northern Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh.

In 2020, fistfights and stone throwing broke out between soldiers from both sides of the border, resulting in fatalities. Last year, the two countries agreed on "peace and tranquillity" along their border in a ten-point document. They also agreed to resume the issuing of tourist visas and to allow direct flights.

Modi stressed that it was necessary for both sides to abide by the agreements and understandings reached on border issues. Both sides were determined to work towards a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable" resolution of the border conflict, he said.

articles.title: Summer wildfires caused 'catastrophic' hidden damage, scientists warn
articles.summary: Bangor University researchers say the scale of damage is far greater than what is immediately visible.
articles.body:
Scientists investigating the damage caused by severe wildfires across Wales this summer say the impact has been "catastrophic".

Extreme heat and exceptionally dry conditions throughout July and August left landscapes such as heathland, moorland and upland grasslands vulnerable to fast spreading fires, resulting in one of the UK's worst wildfire seasons in recent years.

Professor Davey Jones, who is leading a Bangor University survey of several sites across Wales, said the scale of damage was far greater than what was immediately visible.

"People see the blackened vegetation and assume that's the main impact, but the real story is below our feet," said Jones.

During the July peak, fires affected approximately 2,760 acres of countryside across north Wales alone, the equivalent of more than 1,500 football pitches.

At Sychnant Pass in Conwy county, one of the most significant blazes saw 36 homes having to be evacuated and around 200 acres of land affected.

At Sychnant Pass today, there are slight green shoots of recovery visible among the charred hillside.

But Jones described a rare ecosystem housing specialist plants, butterflies and insects, "where the UK is the epicentre globally".

"We've probably lost about 10 centimetres of soil here [at Sychnant Pass] so we've lost all of that organic matter layer.... 4,000 years of carbon gone in a single event," he said.

"Once the topsoil is gone, we can never recover that.

"People see the blackened vegetation and assume that's the main impact, but the real story is below our feet.

"This soil acts as a water sponge, a carbon store, a nutrient bank.

"Losing it is a double whammy, it worsens climate change and makes the habitat far more fragile."

He added, "This site has taken thousands of years to develop and it's all gone in maybe five days? It's incredible.

"If we are going to try and put that soil back, generate artificial soils through the reuse of organic wastes for example, then it's important we understand what the soil quality is now.

"So that we can prepare for the future and design those soils, because they don't exist yet."

Over recent weeks the Bangor team has been racing to collect soil samples at several sites across Wales before heavy winter rainfall washes away the remains.

Their work has included comparing the burnt land with adjacent untouched areas, allowing researchers to measure changes in soil carbon, nutrients, microbial activity, water repellency and erosion risk.

Even NASA satellite data has been used to quickly identify new sites after fires have occurred.

Dr Kara Marsden, a lecturer in soil science who is also working on the project, said working at speed was vital.

"It was really important that we got on site very quickly to measure the soil and vegetation properties while the fire's impacts were still fresh," she said.

"These things can change rapidly, so capturing that baseline data now means we'll have something accurate to compare against in future sampling dates."

She warned that early green shoots now visible at the site did not necessarily reflect true or full recovery.

"Bracken sprouts almost immediately because its rhizomes sit deep in the soil, so the burn layer wouldn't maybe have impacted those" she said.

"But the heather and gorse have much shallower roots, so you know they're completely gone.

"They've been completely lost... that depth of soil they depend on could take thousands of years to form again."

Jones said that the impact of such wildfires extended far beyond biodiversity loss.

"Fires release carbon, nitrogen and sulphur back into the atmosphere, in itself contributing to climate change," he said.

"Every time we have a wildfire, we're just making the problem worse and worse.

"It becomes a self‑sustaining cycle... drier soils, more fires, more carbon released."

He also warned that without rapid restoration and better wildfire preparedness, "we might lose pretty much all of this habitat within our lifetime".

Researchers will return to the sites over the next two years to track recovery and assess whether some habitats are more resilient than others.

Early evidence suggests vegetation can return, but more slowly and more fragile, leaving landscapes increasingly susceptible to future burns.

articles.title: Afghan woman deported from US in first use of secretive 'alien terrorist' court
articles.summary: The legal US resident was never charged with a crime, but was deported due to her family links to terrorism.
articles.body:
An Afghan woman living in Texas with legal US permanent residency has been deported from the country in the first-ever use of a secretive court.

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, chose to leave the US rather than continue to argue her case before the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) and her lawyers.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created in 1996, but had never heard a case before the proceedings in July. It is meant for non-US citizens facing terrorism-related charges when the evidence is confidential and related to national security.

Lawyers for Haji Zada argued that the case violated her right to due process under the US Constitution.

Afghanistan citizen Haji Zada was never charged with a crime, but prosecutors had tried and convicted her son and son-in-law for terror offenses.

Her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhed, were both found guilty of a plot to carry out a mass shooting on Election Day in 2024, inspired by the group calling itself Islamic State

Haji Zada, who has been living in Fort Worth, Texas, was accused by prosecutors of being the "matriarch" of the group, who had worked "to radicalize the family".

In a statement on Friday, the justice department said she "conceded that she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous [immigration] status".

"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.

"Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."

Court-appointed lawyers for Haji Zada said they were denied access to the evidence in her case.

"Our client's choice to consent to removal should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's legitimacy," public defenders Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras said in a statement to The Washington Post.

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process. We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue," they said.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Brics nations Saturday opposed unilateral trade measures such as EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), saying such measures undermine efforts by developing countries aimed at addressing the adverse impacts of climate change.Though they recognised the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to meet climate goals, the grouping’s members sought to delink any unilateral punitive action from achieving a common goal and pitched for energy security for all based on a pragmatic approach where “fossil fuel”, they said, will still play an important role in the world’s energy mix”, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies, in addition to renewable sources and nuclear.CBAM, which entered its operational regime on Jan 1, is a tool to put a price, through imposing a border tax, on carbon-intensive goods, like iron and steel, aluminium and cement, that are entering the 27 EU nations.Though BRICS nations opposed the proposal from the time it was conceived, arguing that the unilateral move placed an additional burden on businesses in developing economies due to embedded emissions in their products, they made their points a part of New Delhi Declaration calling it “punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures that are not in line with international law”.Without any attempt to dilute their respective efforts to meet climate action goals under the Paris Agreement, the nations called for greater actions based on equity and the UN’s principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in light of different national circumstances.They also highlighted the need to enhance energy security by ensuring energy market stability and maintaining undisrupted flows of energy from diverse sources including fossil fuels. Incidentally, four of the BRICS group countries such as Russia, Saudi Arabia, Iran and UAE are among the major global exporters of fossil fuel.Sending a positive signal ahead of COP31, scheduled to take place in Turkey in Nov, they called on all countries to uphold their commitment to maintain and scale up efforts to combat climate change, and expressed their confidence in multilateralism to address the global challenge.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
articles.summary: Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen were adopted from orphanages in Mumbai in the 1980s and grew up in the Netherlands.
articles.body:
Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.

Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.

Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth.

When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.

Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly.

"All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."

Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked.

"They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'.

"And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'.

"At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.

The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.

Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way" .

They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.

Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.

In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook.

Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result.

"I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.

The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match".

"I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister.

"This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."

On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters.

"It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be."

Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs ​and laughter punctuated their ​meeting... followed by their first selfie together".

Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her ⁠DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when ​they first met 30 years ago.

It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters.

"We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know."

Meena and Minal were adopted from different orphanages by two different Dutch couples.

Meena says she grew up in a small village in the Netherlands by parents who taught at a private school.

"They were also my teachers," she says. "They were very loving people, very trusting."

Her father died a few years ago, but her mother continues to live in the same village. "We talk every day. She's still my safe space," she adds.

In 2003, aged 19, Meena had visited the orphanage in Mumbai with her parents and her brother who was adopted from Goa.

They spent two weeks looking through records, trying to find out about Meena's biological parents "because for me it was important to know where I came from. But the orphanage would not reveal any details about them," she says.

Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents.

"Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.

The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says.

"Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."

One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began.

"We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together.

"There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says.

"I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."
